roles.heroLead: Beautiful tile gets the compliments; the membrane behind it earns them. roles.costH2: How much does tile installation cost in Kirkland, WA?
roles.costP1: Price a Kirkland tile project at roughly $14 to $26 for the installed square foot — tile, setting materials, subfloor prep and labor rolled together, the labor piece from $11/sq ft. Standard tub-shower surrounds run you $3,200–$6,800; carried all the way through — floor, shower, niche — most bathrooms invoice at $6,500 to $14,000.
roles.costP2: One truth serves both design and budget: labor tracks the format, never the per-box price. Cuts and grout lines are where handmade-look zellige and small mosaics spend their hours — the mechanism by which a $4 sheet overtakes a $12 large-format porcelain plank on installation day.
roles.costNote: Ranges for Kirkland homes and condos, August 2026 — installed, with tile, materials and labor counted. The written quote from the free estimate is the real figure.
roles.layersLead: Seven layers, stacked in an order that isn't negotiable. When a failed shower around Kirkland gets opened with us watching, some layer is missing — the membrane, near enough always — trimmed out once to bank a few hundred dollars, repaid at five figures when the wall comes apart.
roles.whyP1: No leak introduces itself. Water moves past grout, sits in the substrate, and turns up two years later as a hallway floor with give or a stain blooming on the ceiling of the room below. By that stage the scope reads framing, subfloor, drywall — and the tile you loved, done twice.
roles.whyP2: Call waterproofing 10% of the shower budget. No pricier decision exists in a bathroom remodel than deleting it — nor a less visible one.
roles.scopeIntro: Honest labels: these are starting prices, moved by format, substrate condition and how ambitious the layout gets. The firm figure gets written at your place, at no charge.
roles.cardShower: Waterproofed from the studs out: base pre-sloped, membrane bonded, flood test documented, then the niche, curb or curbless entry, and the tile last. The unglamorous half of the job is the valuable half.
roles.cardFloors: Bathrooms, kitchens, entries, mudrooms, condo baths and basements. Subfloor brought dead flat, and an uncoupling membrane specified where the floor moves or carries radiant heat.
roles.cardBacksplash: Zellige, subway, herringbone, mosaic sheet or slab-look porcelain — outlet cuts kept crisp, edges trimmed properly, grout chosen against your counter, not the tile carton.
roles.cardHeated: Radiant electric mat over an uncoupling membrane, resistance-tested before setting and after grout, on its own circuit. An upgrade that only makes sense while the floor is open.
roles.cardRepair: Cracked field tile, tired grout, shower corners pulling loose. We'll say plainly whether a repair is honest or the substrate behind it has already failed.
roles.cardDemo: Sheeting and negative air go up, then old tile, thinset and backer come down and ride away that same day. Elevator bookings, HOA rules, tight parking — handled without drama.

roles.faqQ1: How much does tile installation cost in Kirkland, WA?
roles.faqA1: Add up tile, setting materials, subfloor prep and labor in Kirkland and installation comes to roughly $14 to $26 for the installed square foot, labor itself starting near $11 per square foot. A standard tub-shower surround will run you $3,200–$6,800; finish the room completely — floor plus shower plus niche — and totals mostly invoice at $6,500 to $14,000. Format outweighs unit price every time: mosaic sheets and large-format planks each consume far more setting labor per square foot than everyday 12×12 tile.
roles.faqQ2: How much does it cost to tile a shower in Kirkland?
roles.faqA2: Tiled showers in Kirkland cost $3,200 to $6,800 for the standard alcove — demolition, bonded waterproofing, a pre-sloped base or pan, setting, niche and grout all included. Designer scope moves the number up: curbless entries, benches, steam enclosures, full-height stone or zellige walls. Waterproofing is only about a tenth of the bill — and it's the tenth that rules out the tens-of-thousands failure.
roles.faqQ3: Do you waterproof showers before tiling?
roles.faqA3: Yes, whatever the tile's ambitions. The build under every shower is a bonded waterproofing system: sloped base, sheet or liquid membrane taken up the walls, sealed seams, corners and penetrations, and a 24-hour flood test we document before setting a single piece. Thinset over cement board does not count as waterproofing. Tile and grout let water straight through — interception is the membrane's job.
roles.faqQ4: How long does a bathroom tile job take?
roles.faqA4: Kirkland bathrooms take four to six working days, condos included. Demolition with dust protection starts it; substrate and waterproofing follow, the 24-hour flood test in the middle; a day or two of setting comes next; grout, silicone and trim wrap it. The first shower waits another 24 hours for the grout to cure. A floor by itself? Usually a two-day matter at most.
roles.faqQ5: Porcelain or ceramic tile — which is better?
roles.faqA5: Different jobs. Porcelain — denser, sub-0.5% water absorption, harder to chip — is the call for floors, showers and any wet or high-traffic surface. Ceramic costs less and looks every bit as good on walls and backsplashes. Our Kirkland rule: porcelain underfoot and in shower floors, always; ceramic, glass or zellige where the surface's whole job is beauty.
roles.faqQ6: Can you install a heated tile floor?
roles.faqA6: Yes. Running $11 to $16 the installed square foot with thermostat within, heated tile is the remodel's best-value indulgence — precisely because it only pencils while the floor is already open. Underneath, the mat sits on uncoupling membrane; resistance gets tested twice, bracketing the setting work; and the circuit it draws from is dedicated to it alone.
roles.faqQ7: Do I need to remove the old tile first?
roles.faqA7: Nearly always, yes. Demolition plus haul-away comes in around $3.50 per square foot and doubles as the only true subfloor inspection — rot, movement and past moisture all show, and the new floor lands at the right height against doorways and cabinetry. Over-tiling can pass on a flat, sound, well-bonded floor, though even then it entombs conditions far better discovered during demo than after grout cures.
roles.faqQ8: How much does a kitchen backsplash cost in Kirkland?
roles.faqA8: A Kirkland backsplash across the typical 30 square feet lands at $1,100 to $2,200 installed, with outlet cuts, trimmed edges and counter-matched grout inside the price. Designer choices — zellige, mosaic sheets, herringbone, a framed feature at the range, slab-look porcelain run to the ceiling — climb the range on layout and cutting time, not because the tile itself must cost more.
roles.faqQ9: Can you fix cracked tile or regrout instead of replacing?
roles.faqA9: Often. From $8 per square foot upward, repair and regrout covers stained or crumbling grout, a couple of tiles cracked by impact, and corners where silicone should replace grout. Where it can't help is a spent substrate — tile sounding hollow, loosening that spreads, softness in the wall — since a patch there buys months at best. Inspection comes first, and you learn which situation is yours before any quote exists.
roles.faqQ10: Which Kirkland neighborhoods do you tile?
roles.faqA10: All of Kirkland — Moss Bay, Market, Norkirk, Highlands, Everest, Lakeview, Central Houghton, Carillon Point, Bridle Trails, North and South Rose Hill, Kingsgate, Totem Lake, North and South Juanita and Finn Hill — condos downtown included, plus Bellevue, Redmond, Bothell, Kenmore, Woodinville and the rest of the Eastside and Seattle.
roles.faqQ11: What warranty comes with tile installation?
roles.faqA11: Every OC Flooring tile installation carries a 2-year workmanship warranty — twice the term we give carpet, because tile defects show themselves in year two, not week two. When the shower uses a manufacturer's full waterproofing assembly, their system warranty adds to ours. Membrane and flood test are photographed on every job, so the record is there for a future appraisal or sale.
